snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The arch-dogmatist: the Preface calls Christianity "Platonism for 'the people'" and blames Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself for the worst error philosophy has made; later chapters return to his death-bed reading (a book of Aristophanes, not scripture) and the "Socratism" smuggled into his own morality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The dialectician whose "Will to Truth" the book keeps circling back to -- the Sphinx he and Nietzsche's readers both face in the Preface, the man Plato may have caught his morality from, and the ironist whose real deception (per Chapter 6) was persuading reason to defend the instincts it pretended to rule.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher whose joke about Plato and the Platonists -- calling them "Dionysiokolakes," flatterers of the tyrant Dionysius -- opens Chapter 1's gallery of philosophers' malice; his own three hundred garden-written books earned him a hundred years of obscurity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius of Syracuse
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Syracuse behind Plato's visits and Epicurus's coinage "Dionysiokolakes" (flatterers of Dionysius) -- named only in that etymology, not the god Dionysus of Chapter 10's closing confession.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Immanuel Kant
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose Table of Categories and "synthetic judgment a priori" Chapter 1 dissects at length as a comic non-answer ("by means of a means"); later called "the great Chinaman of Konigsberg," and named again for his rift with Hume and his categorical imperative.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baruch Spinoza
snapshots.body: The philosopher accused of smuggling self-preservation in as a "superfluous" teleological principle; later cited for the "no-more-laughing and no-more-weeping" of his ethics, and, in Chapter 2, grouped with Giordano Bruno as a persecuted recluse whose hidden vengefulness is worth reading his own theology to find.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Roger Boscovich
snapshots.body: The Croatian physicist ("the Pole Boscovich" in this telling), credited with Copernicus as the greatest opponent of ocular evidence -- his refutation of atomism is called the greatest triumph over the senses yet achieved.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Boscovich as the other great "Pole" who persuaded humanity to believe, against the senses, that the earth does not stand still.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
snapshots.body: Credited with christening "intellectual intuition" during German philosophy's post-Kantian honeymoon; quoted again in Chapter 9 dismissing Locke in three French words, "Je meprise Locke."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Giordano Bruno
snapshots.body: The philosopher burned for heresy, grouped with Spinoza in Chapter 2 as one of the "compulsory recluses" whose long persecution breeds concealed vengeance-seeking beneath even the most intellectual disguise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baron Munchausen
snapshots.body: Raspe's tall-tale baron, invoked for the image of pulling oneself into existence "by the hair, out of the slough of nothingness" -- Nietzsche's figure for the self-contradiction at the heart of wanting to be one's own cause.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rene Descartes
snapshots.body: The father of rationalism, credited (via Kant's defiance of him) with modern philosophy's covert war on the Christian soul, and later dismissed in one line as superficial, since reason is only a tool.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moliere
snapshots.body: Cited for the doctor's mock-answer in his plays -- opium causes sleep "by means of a means," the virtus dormitiva -- Nietzsche's model for the comic non-explanation he accuses Kant of repeating.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
snapshots.body: The one German prose stylist exempted from the charge that German cannot manage a swift TEMPO -- his histrionic range, translation of Bayle, and debt to Diderot and Voltaire let him love "free-spiritism" in style as well as thought.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pierre Bayle
snapshots.body: The skeptic philosophe whose work Lessing translated -- cited in passing as one of the influences Lessing absorbed on his way to a livelier German prose.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Denis Diderot
snapshots.body: The Encyclopedist in whose shadow Lessing "took refuge" -- one of the French influences credited with loosening German prose's otherwise leaden pace.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
snapshots.body: Author of The Principe, praised for a TEMPO so fast it "makes us breathe the dry, fine air of Florence" even while narrating the gravest matters in a boisterous gallop -- the untranslatable opposite of German heaviness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Petronius
snapshots.body: The Roman satirist called the greatest master of PRESTO in invention and language "hitherto" -- untranslatable into German, Nietzsche says, for the same reason Aristophanes is.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophanes
snapshots.body: The comic playwright found, in a much-repeated anecdote, under Plato's pillow on his deathbed instead of any scripture -- proof, for Nietzsche, that even Plato could not have endured a Greek life without him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ferdinando Galiani
snapshots.body: The Neapolitan abbe called "the profoundest, acutest, and perhaps also filthiest man of his century": quoter of the witticism about Helvetius, source of a letter to Madame d'Epinay on Europe's uglifying, and one of Chapter 10's examples (with Hamlet) of a mask concealing a broken, proud heart.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Martin Luther
snapshots.body: Named among the northern barbarians of the spirit whose slave-faith Nietzsche distinguishes from Pascal's more terrible, suicidal reason; his Bible is later called the one masterpiece of German prose, next to which almost everything else is "merely literature."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oliver Cromwell
snapshots.body: Named alongside Luther as a northern barbarian of the spirit whose faith, unlike Pascal's, was a plain, austere slave-faith rather than a continuous suicide of reason.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Blaise Pascal
snapshots.body: The exemplary Christian intellect: his faith is called a "continuous suicide of reason," his intellectual conscience the measure by which any psychologist of homines religiosi would have to be judged, and his own tortured self-mutilation the case study Nietzsche imagines a "divine hammer" confronting at the chapter's close.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saint Augustine
snapshots.body: The "holy rhetorician" quoted for his phrase "Sabbath of Sabbaths" describing the peace a war-torn soul craves, and later cited for an Oriental exaltation of mind that, like a favored slave's, lacks all nobility of bearing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame Guyon
snapshots.body: The French mystic whose passion for God Nietzsche calls feminine and sensual, longing unconsciously for a union at once mystical and physical -- one of his three types of religious devotion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Auguste Comte
snapshots.body: Founder of positivist sociology, whose system strikes Nietzsche as startlingly Catholic and un-German in its Roman logic, evidence of how deeply Latin races remain attached to Catholicism even in unbelief.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve
snapshots.body: The critic called an "amiable and shrewd cicerone of Port Royal" -- Jesuitical in manner despite his hostility to Jesuits, one of the later French skeptics whose Celtic blood still shows through as piety.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ernest Renan
snapshots.body: The historian of religion whose sentence claiming religion as the product of the "normal man" Nietzsche quotes at length in French, calls religious naivete par excellence, and then admits he has come to enjoy for how thoroughly it inverts his own view.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tiberius
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor whose human sacrifice in the Mithra-Grotto on Capri is called the most terrible of all Roman anachronisms -- an example of religious cruelty's first, most literal rung.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Buddha
snapshots.body: Invoked as the one earlier thinker who, like Schopenhauer, still looked beyond good and evil while remaining under the "dominion and delusion of morality"; also credited alongside Christianity with teaching even the lowest to bear a difficult life through piety.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kundry
snapshots.body: The character from Wagner's Parsifal in whom Wagner staged the "terrible and eternal type" of the religious neurosis -- proof, for Nietzsche, of how thoroughly Schopenhauerian Wagner's own final work became.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Franco Sacchetti
snapshots.body: The medieval Florentine novelliere credited by citation ("Nov. 86") as the source of the Italian proverb about good and bad women alike needing the stick -- one of the epigrams collected "from old Florentine novels, moreover, from life."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jesus
snapshots.body: Quoted telling his fellow Jews that the law was only for servants and that he loves God as a son; much later, imagined by the psychologist as a soul so insatiable for love that it had to invent both a hell for those who refused him and a God who is entire love, out of pity for how paltry human love actually is.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eros
snapshots.body: The god of love, personified in one epigram as having been given poison to drink by Christianity -- he did not die of it, Nietzsche says, but degenerated into Vice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ulysses
snapshots.body: The hero who, in one epigram, parts from Nausicaa "blessing it rather than in love with it" -- Nietzsche's model for how to part from life itself; invoked again in Chapter 9 as the "stopped Ulysses-ears" of the disciplined man of knowledge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nausicaa
snapshots.body: The Phaeacian princess from whom Ulysses parts at the end of his stay on her island -- the epigram's figure for a clean, unsentimental leave-taking from something one no longer needs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Circe
snapshots.body: The enchantress invoked twice as a figure of seductive, dangerous knowledge: once as a fellow philosopher alongside the Sphinx in Chapter 7's meditation on skepticism, once as the name Nietzsche gives outright to cruelty's own "philtre" in Chapter 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hafiz
snapshots.body: The Persian poet named, with Goethe, as an example of surrendering wholly and wantonly to the emotions -- one of Chapter 6's short catalogue of moral systems as disguised expediency.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cesare Borgia
snapshots.body: The Renaissance "beast and man of prey" Nietzsche offers as an example that moralists mistake for a monster rather than the healthiest kind of tropical growth -- original-en spells him "Caesar Borgia," modern-en the Italian "Cesare Borgia."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julius Caesar
snapshots.body: Named alongside Alcibiades as one of the finest examples of a rare type: men whose inherited, unresolved contrariety of instinct becomes, rather than weakness, an additional spur to conquest.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcibiades
snapshots.body: Named alongside Julius Caesar as the finest example, with him, of a man whose contradictory inheritance sharpens rather than weakens his drive to conquer and outmaneuver others.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frederick II of Hohenstaufen
snapshots.body: The medieval Holy Roman Emperor Nietzsche calls "the first of Europeans" by his own taste, named alongside Alcibiades, Caesar and Leonardo as a man whose inherited contrariety became conquering strength -- a different Frederick from Chapter 7's Frederick the Great.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonardo da Vinci
snapshots.body: Named, among artists, as sharing the same rare temperament as Alcibiades, Julius Caesar and Frederick II: one whose unresolved inner contrariety becomes a spur rather than a weakness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catiline
snapshots.body: The Roman conspirator ("Catalina" in original-en's spelling) named alongside Cagliostro as an example of the "higher arts" one might use to try to possess an entire nation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alessandro Cagliostro
snapshots.body: The eighteenth-century adventurer and impostor, named alongside Catiline as an example of the arts of possessing a nation, and later invoked as the type of "philosophical Cagliostro" the philosopher risks becoming if he loses self-respect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tacitus
snapshots.body: The Roman historian cited, with "the whole ancient world," for calling the Jews a people "born for slavery" -- the received verdict Nietzsche sets against the Jews' own self-conception as chosen, before crediting them with inverting all values.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: George Sand
snapshots.body: The novelist (born Amantine Dupin, published under the pen name "Monsieur George Sand") named at 8:19 with Madame de Stael and Madame Roland as one of three women no one should cite in favor of "woman as she is" -- a different Sand from Chapter 9's Karl Ludwig Sand, distinguished only by location.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Karl Ludwig Sand
snapshots.body: The nationalist student who assassinated the playwright Kotzebue in 1819, named only as "Sand" at 9:4 in the same dark joke about Kotzebue's own boast that he "knew his Germans" -- a different Sand from Chapter 6's novelist George Sand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: August von Kotzebue
snapshots.body: The popular playwright whose boast that he "knew his Germans" sets up the darkly ironic mention of Sand -- the nationalist student who assassinated him -- as someone who thought he knew them too.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean Paul
snapshots.body: The pen name of Johann Paul Friedrich Richter, cited for having seen through Fichte's patriotic flattery of the Germans even though Goethe, Nietzsche guesses, judged the Germans differently.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose "lying but patriotic flatteries and exaggerations" about the German character Jean Paul is credited with seeing through.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
snapshots.body: Repeatedly paired with Napoleon as one of the "good Europeans": his prose is granted one exception to German stylistic clumsiness, his rewriting of Faust is tied to Napoleon's rise, his remark to Rath Schlosser on true esteem is quoted directly, and Napoleon's own astonishment on meeting him ("Voila un homme!") closes Chapter 7's parable of German skepticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
snapshots.body: Named again and again as the culmination of a European drama: the "absolute ruler" Europe's herd instinct craved, the man whose appearance changed Goethe's own Faust, the figure before whom Europe "danced round the Tree of Liberty" and then fell in adoration, and the one who told Madame de Stael to be silent in politics.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
snapshots.body: Named with Kant as one of the "philosophical workers" who systematize existing values rather than create new ones; also credited with having systematized the very riddles of the German soul that Wagner then set to music, and blamed by Schopenhauer's unintelligent rage for severing a whole generation from German culture.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heraclitus
snapshots.body: Named, with Plato and Empedocles, among the "royal and magnificent anchorites of the spirit" whose style of philosophy Nietzsche contrasts with the two "lions of Berlin" who pass for philosophers today.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Empedocles
snapshots.body: Named alongside Heraclitus and Plato as one of the ancient anchorites of the spirit against whom the modern philosophical pretenders of Berlin are measured and found wanting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugen Duhring
snapshots.body: One of the "two lions of Berlin" -- called "the anarchist" -- held up as an example of the hotch-potch "realist" or "positivist" philosophy that has replaced genuine philosophizing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eduard von Hartmann
snapshots.body: The other "lion of Berlin" -- called "the amalgamist" -- named alongside Eugen Duhring as an example of the diminished philosophy now passing for the real thing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
snapshots.body: Quoted for his motto "je ne meprise presque rien" (I despise almost nothing) -- Nietzsche's example of the "objective" or purely reflective spirit that affirms and denies nothing of its own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Michel de Montaigne
snapshots.body: Quoted for his signature question "What do I know?" -- one of the skeptic's consoling formulas, alongside Socrates' "I know that I know nothing."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jules Michelet
snapshots.body: The French historian credited with the phrase describing the German spirit as "cet esprit fataliste, ironique, mephistophelique" -- quoted as the outside verdict on a distinctly German kind of skepticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frederick the Great
snapshots.body: The King of Prussia whose "problematic, crazy father" doubted his manliness -- Nietzsche's parable for a new, harder, more dangerous German skepticism first entering Germany "in the person of the great Frederick"; a different Frederick from Chapter 6's Frederick II of Hohenstaufen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gustave Flaubert
snapshots.body: The "honest citizen of Rouen" whose lifelong preoccupation with bourgeois stupidity -- betise bourgeoise -- Nietzsche calls a mode of self-torment and refined cruelty.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame d'Epinay
snapshots.body: The addressee of a thoughtful letter from Galiani, cited as early documentary evidence of the overshadowing and "uglifying" of Europe that Nietzsche traces across the nineteenth century.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles de Saint-Evremond
snapshots.body: The seventeenth-century French critic named among those who could not fully appropriate Homer, reproaching him for his "esprit vaste" -- part of Nietzsche's argument that only the modern, hybrid "historical sense" can enjoy Homer without reservation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Voltaire
snapshots.body: Named repeatedly as the last echo of the classicizing century that still could not fully enjoy Homer; earlier apostrophized directly ("O Voltaire! O humanity! O idiocy!") over the naive idea that seeking truth serves the good.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The poet the modern "historical sense" can finally enjoy in full, where classical French taste (Saint-Evremond, Voltaire) could not -- Chapter 8's central test case for what a truly hybrid, omnivorous culture can appreciate that a purer one cannot.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Shakespeare
snapshots.body: Called a "marvelous Spanish-Moorish-Saxon synthesis of taste" that an ancient Athenian would have found laughable -- another of Chapter 8's proofs that only the modern, semi-barbarian European can enjoy such motley art without disturbance.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeschylus
snapshots.body: Named as part of the "circle" of ancient Athenian taste against which Shakespeare's motley style is measured -- original-en's odd spelling "AEschylus" and modern-en's "Aeschylus" name the same Greek tragedian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jeremy Bentham
snapshots.body: The utilitarian philosopher whose footsteps English moralists are said to "stalk" in, just as he had earlier stalked in the footsteps of Helvetius -- part of Chapter 8's dismissal of English moral philosophy as tedious.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Claude Adrien Helvetius
snapshots.body: The Enlightenment philosopher Bentham is said to have followed -- quoted secondhand via Galiani's witticism calling him "ce senateur Pococurante" (that senator who cares for nothing), borrowing the name of Voltaire's blase character in Candide rather than naming a real Pococurante.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame de Lambert
snapshots.body: The eighteenth-century salon hostess whose remark to her son -- "never permit yourself follies except ones that will give you great pleasure" -- Nietzsche calls the wisest and most motherly thing ever said to a son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dante Alighieri
snapshots.body: Named with Goethe as sharing a belief about woman that Nietzsche expects every noble woman to reject -- quoted in the original Italian, "Ella guardava suso, ed io in lei."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame de Stael
snapshots.body: The writer Napoleon is said to have told, in Latin, to keep quiet in politics ("mulier taceat in politicis"); also one of three women (with Madame Roland and George Sand) a woman should not cite as proof of her sex's capacities.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame Roland
snapshots.body: The French revolutionary-era writer named, with Madame de Stael and George Sand, as one of "three comical women" no one should cite as an argument for feminine emancipation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: David Hume
snapshots.body: The skeptic Kant is said to have risen up against; named, with Hobbes and Locke, among the three Englishmen whose mechanical philosophy Nietzsche blames for a century of philosophical abasement.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thomas Hobbes
snapshots.body: Named with Hume and Locke as one of the three Englishmen responsible for depreciating the very idea of "philosopher"; quoted again in Chapter 10 for calling laughter a "bad infirmity of human nature."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Locke
snapshots.body: Named at 2:19 for a "superficiality" about the origin of ideas Nietzsche says his own account corrects, and again at 9:12 with Hobbes and Hume as one of the English trio blamed for abasing philosophy -- quoted secondhand there via Schelling's dismissive French, "Je meprise Locke."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thomas Carlyle
snapshots.body: Called "the absurd muddle-head" and "half-actor and rhetorician" whose passionate grimaces conceal exactly what England lacks: real depth of intellect, i.e. philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Francis Bacon
snapshots.body: Named as representing, by himself, an "attack on the philosophical spirit generally" -- the opening figure in Chapter 9's roll call of English thinkers Nietzsche holds responsible for depreciating philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demosthenes
snapshots.body: Named with Cicero as an orator whose long, breath-spanning periods -- possible only because ancient audiences still read aloud -- modern readers, short of breath in every sense, no longer have any right to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.body: Named with Demosthenes as a master of the classical, breath-defined period, part of Chapter 9's argument that German prose has lost its ear because Germans no longer read aloud.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles Darwin
snapshots.body: Named, with John Stuart Mill and Herbert Spencer, as one of the "respectable but mediocre Englishmen" whose ascendancy in European taste Nietzsche treats as symptomatic rather than triumphant, even while granting that English narrowness suited his specific discoveries.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Stuart Mill
snapshots.body: Named with Darwin and Herbert Spencer as one of the mediocre Englishmen whose truths appeal specifically to mediocre minds.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Herbert Spencer
snapshots.body: Named with Darwin and Mill as the third of Chapter 9's mediocre but ascendant Englishmen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich von Sybel
snapshots.body: The German historian named, pluralized ("the Sybels"), as one type-example of the "Prussian folly" -- historians with, Nietzsche says, "closely bandaged heads."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich von Treitschke
snapshots.body: The nationalist historian named, pluralized ("the Treitschkes"), alongside Sybel as the other type-example of Prussian historical folly.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich Heine
snapshots.body: Named as having been "reincarnated" in the refined, fastidious lyrists of Paris -- one of the German exports France has quietly absorbed -- and later grouped among the "good Europeans" whose real allegiance outran their fatherlands.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippolyte Taine
snapshots.body: The French historian in whose work Hegel's influence is said now to exercise an almost tyrannical dominance over French thought -- called "the first of living historians."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Victor Hugo
snapshots.body: The writer whose funeral is cited as the occasion for a "veritable orgy of bad taste" and national self-admiration, evidence for Nietzsche of France's current besottedness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stendhal
snapshots.body: The pen name of Henri Beyle, called "the last great psychologist of France": named as Stendhal for his aphorism that a good philosopher must be dry, clear, without illusion (Chapter 3), and as Henri Beyle for his Napoleonic tempo in surveying the European soul two generations ahead of his readers (Chapter 9).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Richard Wagner
snapshots.body: The composer whose overture to the Meistersinger opens Chapter 9's long study of German music; his Kundry (Chapter 3) staged the religious neurosis as Schopenhauerian confession, his riddles of the German soul are said to be the ones Hegel had already systematized, and the chapter's climax names him -- alongside Napoleon and Goethe -- among the handful of true "good Europeans," his Siegfried and Parsifal both weighed at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
snapshots.body: Contrasted at length with Mozart as the "intermediate event" between an old mellow soul and a future over-young one -- his music carries, Nietzsche says, the same twilight of loss and hope in which Europe dreamed with Rousseau and danced toward Napoleon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
snapshots.body: Called the last echo of a great, centuries-old European taste -- his rococo delicacy, tenderness, and belief in the South are said still to speak to something left in "us," unlike Beethoven's more fragile appeal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
snapshots.body: Named as the starting point of the historical arc Beethoven's music is said to carry -- Europe "dreamed with Rousseau" before dancing around the Tree of Liberty and falling into adoration of Napoleon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Friedrich Schiller
snapshots.body: Named among the poets (with Rousseau, Shelley and Byron) whose language now sounds strange to modern ears despite once voicing the same European fate Beethoven's music sang; a footnote in original-en also traces one phrase to his play William Tell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
snapshots.body: Named with Rousseau, Schiller and Byron as one of the Romantic poets whose collective voice, once able to speak Europe's fate, now sounds difficult to fully grasp.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lord Byron
snapshots.body: Named among the Romantic poets whose voice has faded from modern ears; his Manfred is also the basis for the Schumann composition Nietzsche calls a "mistake and a misunderstanding," and he appears again in Chapter 10 among the great poets whose "work" invented the men later reverenced as their authors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Carl Maria von Weber
snapshots.body: The composer of Der Freischutz and Oberon, named as belonging to a Romanticism already extinct, though not yet forgotten, in German music.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich Marschner
snapshots.body: The composer of Hans Heiling and Der Vampyr, grouped with Weber as another representative of the fading Romantic school of German opera.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Felix Mendelssohn
snapshots.body: Called "that halcyon master," whose lighter, purer, happier soul won quick admiration and was just as quickly forgotten -- the "beautiful episode" of German music.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robert Schumann
snapshots.body: The composer treated at length as the point where German music became merely national rather than European: his Manfred is called a mistake, his taste "fundamentally petty," and his "surmounting" a relief precisely because it ends a danger Beethoven and Mozart never posed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Siegfried
snapshots.body: The hero of Wagner's Ring, called Wagner's most remarkable, permanently inimitable creation -- "too free, too hard, too cheerful, too healthy" for the taste of older, more mellow civilizations, and, Nietzsche says, almost a sin against Romanticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugene Delacroix
snapshots.body: Named as the artist nearest related to Wagner among the great European Romantics -- grouped with Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heine and Schopenhauer as one who outgrew any single fatherland.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Honore de Balzac
snapshots.body: Cited near the start of Chapter 7 for the phrase "montrer ses plaies" (to show one's wounds); named again in Chapter 9 as an example of the tireless, self-destroying worker unable to achieve a noble tempo or lento in life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Georges Bizet
snapshots.body: The composer credited with having made music "for" the "good Europeans" who love both North and South at once -- his work is called the discovery of "a piece of the South in music."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
snapshots.body: Discussed at greater length than almost anyone else in the book: his account of the will is picked apart in Chapter 1, his pessimism is the background of Chapter 3's religious crisis (with Wagner's Kundry its "genuine Schopenhauerian consequence"), Chapter 6 quotes his Grundprobleme der Ethik at length and notes, drily, that this repudiator of God still played the flute every day after dinner, and Chapter 9 counts him among the true "good Europeans."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rath Schlosser
snapshots.body: Johann Georg Schlosser, Goethe's brother-in-law and the addressee of the letter Nietzsche quotes as Chapter 10's epigraph: "One can only truly esteem him who does not look out for himself."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Raphael
snapshots.body: Invoked in the phrase "Raphael without hands" -- Nietzsche's figure for genius that lacks the sheer number of hands needed to seize the right moment.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Horace
snapshots.body: Quoted in Latin ("naturam expellere... usque recurret") on the impossibility of driving out nature with a pitchfork -- cited as the source any truthfulness-preaching educator would eventually have to reach for.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dr. Marianus
snapshots.body: The character from Goethe's Faust, Part II, whose line -- "Here is the prospect free, the mind exalted" -- is quoted (with attribution given only in a footnote) to introduce the reverse kind of man who is also on a height but looks downward.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysus
snapshots.body: The god who names himself only near the close of Chapter 10 as "the tempter-god and born rat-catcher of consciences" -- Nietzsche's own last disciple and initiate, distinct from the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse named in Chapter 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariadne
snapshots.body: Named as present at Dionysus's side when the god confesses, "under certain circumstances I love mankind" -- the mythic consort Nietzsche would return to repeatedly in his later notebooks.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Sphinx
snapshots.body: The riddling monster of the Oedipus myth, twice personified as a figure of dangerous, ambiguous knowledge -- "which of us is the Oedipus here? Which the Sphinx?" in the Preface's opening pages, and "the Sphinx, too, is a Circe" in Chapter 7.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oedipus
snapshots.body: Named twice as the figure of fearless, unblinking insight: paired with the Sphinx in the Preface's opening question about who is asking whom, and again in Chapter 8's image of "fearless Oedipus-eyes" turned on nature itself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zarathustra
snapshots.body: Nietzsche's own prophet-figure from Thus Spoke Zarathustra, named in the closing poem's final stanza as the long-awaited "Guest of Guests" whose arrival ends the poem's long, lonely waiting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: Named for the constellation, not the labors: Nietzsche says he is pleased to hear the sun is moving rapidly toward it, and hopes "good Europeans" will do likewise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wotan
snapshots.body: The Norse/Germanic god quoted via an old Scandinavian saga -- "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast" -- Nietzsche's chosen epigraph for the proud, self-mastering Viking soul at the center of master-morality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pallas Athene
snapshots.body: The Greek goddess invoked as the figure Spinoza's mathematical "mail and mask" was meant to terrify any assailant away from approaching, as though she were an "invincible maiden."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The arch-dogmatist: the Preface calls Christianity "Platonism for 'the people'" and blames Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself for the worst error philosophy has made; later chapters return to his death-bed reading (a book of Aristophanes, not scripture) and the "Socratism" smuggled into his own morality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The dialectician whose "Will to Truth" the book keeps circling back to -- the Sphinx he and Nietzsche's readers both face in the Preface, the man Plato may have caught his morality from, and the ironist whose real deception (per Chapter 6) was persuading reason to defend the instincts it pretended to rule.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The Greek philosopher whose joke about Plato and the Platonists -- calling them "Dionysiokolakes," flatterers of the tyrant Dionysius -- opens Chapter 1's gallery of philosophers' malice; his own three hundred garden-written books earned him a hundred years of obscurity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysius of Syracuse
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Syracuse behind Plato's visits and Epicurus's coinage "Dionysiokolakes" (flatterers of Dionysius) -- named only in that etymology, not the god Dionysus of Chapter 10's closing confession.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Immanuel Kant
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose Table of Categories and "synthetic judgment a priori" Chapter 1 dissects at length as a comic non-answer ("by means of a means"); later called "the great Chinaman of Konigsberg," and named again for his rift with Hume and his categorical imperative.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baruch Spinoza
snapshots.body: The philosopher accused of smuggling self-preservation in as a "superfluous" teleological principle; later cited for the "no-more-laughing and no-more-weeping" of his ethics, and, in Chapter 2, grouped with Giordano Bruno as a persecuted recluse whose hidden vengefulness is worth reading his own theology to find.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Roger Boscovich
snapshots.body: The Croatian physicist ("the Pole Boscovich" in this telling), credited with Copernicus as the greatest opponent of ocular evidence -- his refutation of atomism is called the greatest triumph over the senses yet achieved.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Boscovich as the other great "Pole" who persuaded humanity to believe, against the senses, that the earth does not stand still.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
snapshots.body: Credited with christening "intellectual intuition" during German philosophy's post-Kantian honeymoon; quoted again in Chapter 9 dismissing Locke in three French words, "Je meprise Locke."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Giordano Bruno
snapshots.body: The philosopher burned for heresy, grouped with Spinoza in Chapter 2 as one of the "compulsory recluses" whose long persecution breeds concealed vengeance-seeking beneath even the most intellectual disguise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Baron Munchausen
snapshots.body: Raspe's tall-tale baron, invoked for the image of pulling oneself into existence "by the hair, out of the slough of nothingness" -- Nietzsche's figure for the self-contradiction at the heart of wanting to be one's own cause.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rene Descartes
snapshots.body: The father of rationalism, credited (via Kant's defiance of him) with modern philosophy's covert war on the Christian soul, and later dismissed in one line as superficial, since reason is only a tool.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Moliere
snapshots.body: Cited for the doctor's mock-answer in his plays -- opium causes sleep "by means of a means," the virtus dormitiva -- Nietzsche's model for the comic non-explanation he accuses Kant of repeating.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
snapshots.body: The one German prose stylist exempted from the charge that German cannot manage a swift TEMPO -- his histrionic range, translation of Bayle, and debt to Diderot and Voltaire let him love "free-spiritism" in style as well as thought.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pierre Bayle
snapshots.body: The skeptic philosophe whose work Lessing translated -- cited in passing as one of the influences Lessing absorbed on his way to a livelier German prose.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Denis Diderot
snapshots.body: The Encyclopedist in whose shadow Lessing "took refuge" -- one of the French influences credited with loosening German prose's otherwise leaden pace.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
snapshots.body: Author of The Principe, praised for a TEMPO so fast it "makes us breathe the dry, fine air of Florence" even while narrating the gravest matters in a boisterous gallop -- the untranslatable opposite of German heaviness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Petronius
snapshots.body: The Roman satirist called the greatest master of PRESTO in invention and language "hitherto" -- untranslatable into German, Nietzsche says, for the same reason Aristophanes is.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristophanes
snapshots.body: The comic playwright found, in a much-repeated anecdote, under Plato's pillow on his deathbed instead of any scripture -- proof, for Nietzsche, that even Plato could not have endured a Greek life without him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ferdinando Galiani
snapshots.body: The Neapolitan abbe called "the profoundest, acutest, and perhaps also filthiest man of his century": quoter of the witticism about Helvetius, source of a letter to Madame d'Epinay on Europe's uglifying, and one of Chapter 10's examples (with Hamlet) of a mask concealing a broken, proud heart.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Martin Luther
snapshots.body: Named among the northern barbarians of the spirit whose slave-faith Nietzsche distinguishes from Pascal's more terrible, suicidal reason; his Bible is later called the one masterpiece of German prose, next to which almost everything else is "merely literature."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oliver Cromwell
snapshots.body: Named alongside Luther as a northern barbarian of the spirit whose faith, unlike Pascal's, was a plain, austere slave-faith rather than a continuous suicide of reason.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Blaise Pascal
snapshots.body: The exemplary Christian intellect: his faith is called a "continuous suicide of reason," his intellectual conscience the measure by which any psychologist of homines religiosi would have to be judged, and his own tortured self-mutilation the case study Nietzsche imagines a "divine hammer" confronting at the chapter's close.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saint Augustine
snapshots.body: The "holy rhetorician" quoted for his phrase "Sabbath of Sabbaths" describing the peace a war-torn soul craves, and later cited for an Oriental exaltation of mind that, like a favored slave's, lacks all nobility of bearing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame Guyon
snapshots.body: The French mystic whose passion for God Nietzsche calls feminine and sensual, longing unconsciously for a union at once mystical and physical -- one of his three types of religious devotion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Auguste Comte
snapshots.body: Founder of positivist sociology, whose system strikes Nietzsche as startlingly Catholic and un-German in its Roman logic, evidence of how deeply Latin races remain attached to Catholicism even in unbelief.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles Augustin Sainte-Beuve
snapshots.body: The critic called an "amiable and shrewd cicerone of Port Royal" -- Jesuitical in manner despite his hostility to Jesuits, one of the later French skeptics whose Celtic blood still shows through as piety.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ernest Renan
snapshots.body: The historian of religion whose sentence claiming religion as the product of the "normal man" Nietzsche quotes at length in French, calls religious naivete par excellence, and then admits he has come to enjoy for how thoroughly it inverts his own view.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tiberius
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor whose human sacrifice in the Mithra-Grotto on Capri is called the most terrible of all Roman anachronisms -- an example of religious cruelty's first, most literal rung.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Buddha
snapshots.body: Invoked as the one earlier thinker who, like Schopenhauer, still looked beyond good and evil while remaining under the "dominion and delusion of morality"; also credited alongside Christianity with teaching even the lowest to bear a difficult life through piety.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kundry
snapshots.body: The character from Wagner's Parsifal in whom Wagner staged the "terrible and eternal type" of the religious neurosis -- proof, for Nietzsche, of how thoroughly Schopenhauerian Wagner's own final work became.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Franco Sacchetti
snapshots.body: The medieval Florentine novelliere credited by citation ("Nov. 86") as the source of the Italian proverb about good and bad women alike needing the stick -- one of the epigrams collected "from old Florentine novels, moreover, from life."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jesus
snapshots.body: Quoted telling his fellow Jews that the law was only for servants and that he loves God as a son; much later, imagined by the psychologist as a soul so insatiable for love that it had to invent both a hell for those who refused him and a God who is entire love, out of pity for how paltry human love actually is.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eros
snapshots.body: The god of love, personified in one epigram as having been given poison to drink by Christianity -- he did not die of it, Nietzsche says, but degenerated into Vice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ulysses
snapshots.body: The hero who, in one epigram, parts from Nausicaa "blessing it rather than in love with it" -- Nietzsche's model for how to part from life itself; invoked again in Chapter 9 as the "stopped Ulysses-ears" of the disciplined man of knowledge.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nausicaa
snapshots.body: The Phaeacian princess from whom Ulysses parts at the end of his stay on her island -- the epigram's figure for a clean, unsentimental leave-taking from something one no longer needs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Circe
snapshots.body: The enchantress invoked twice as a figure of seductive, dangerous knowledge: once as a fellow philosopher alongside the Sphinx in Chapter 7's meditation on skepticism, once as the name Nietzsche gives outright to cruelty's own "philtre" in Chapter 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hafiz
snapshots.body: The Persian poet named, with Goethe, as an example of surrendering wholly and wantonly to the emotions -- one of Chapter 6's short catalogue of moral systems as disguised expediency.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cesare Borgia
snapshots.body: The Renaissance "beast and man of prey" Nietzsche offers as an example that moralists mistake for a monster rather than the healthiest kind of tropical growth -- original-en spells him "Caesar Borgia," modern-en the Italian "Cesare Borgia."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julius Caesar
snapshots.body: Named alongside Alcibiades as one of the finest examples of a rare type: men whose inherited, unresolved contrariety of instinct becomes, rather than weakness, an additional spur to conquest.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcibiades
snapshots.body: Named alongside Julius Caesar as the finest example, with him, of a man whose contradictory inheritance sharpens rather than weakens his drive to conquer and outmaneuver others.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frederick II of Hohenstaufen
snapshots.body: The medieval Holy Roman Emperor Nietzsche calls "the first of Europeans" by his own taste, named alongside Alcibiades, Caesar and Leonardo as a man whose inherited contrariety became conquering strength -- a different Frederick from Chapter 7's Frederick the Great.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonardo da Vinci
snapshots.body: Named, among artists, as sharing the same rare temperament as Alcibiades, Julius Caesar and Frederick II: one whose unresolved inner contrariety becomes a spur rather than a weakness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catiline
snapshots.body: The Roman conspirator ("Catalina" in original-en's spelling) named alongside Cagliostro as an example of the "higher arts" one might use to try to possess an entire nation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alessandro Cagliostro
snapshots.body: The eighteenth-century adventurer and impostor, named alongside Catiline as an example of the arts of possessing a nation, and later invoked as the type of "philosophical Cagliostro" the philosopher risks becoming if he loses self-respect.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tacitus
snapshots.body: The Roman historian cited, with "the whole ancient world," for calling the Jews a people "born for slavery" -- the received verdict Nietzsche sets against the Jews' own self-conception as chosen, before crediting them with inverting all values.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: George Sand
snapshots.body: The novelist (born Amantine Dupin, published under the pen name "Monsieur George Sand") named at 8:19 with Madame de Stael and Madame Roland as one of three women no one should cite in favor of "woman as she is" -- a different Sand from Chapter 9's Karl Ludwig Sand, distinguished only by location.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Karl Ludwig Sand
snapshots.body: The nationalist student who assassinated the playwright Kotzebue in 1819, named only as "Sand" at 9:4 in the same dark joke about Kotzebue's own boast that he "knew his Germans" -- a different Sand from Chapter 6's novelist George Sand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: August von Kotzebue
snapshots.body: The popular playwright whose boast that he "knew his Germans" sets up the darkly ironic mention of Sand -- the nationalist student who assassinated him -- as someone who thought he knew them too.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean Paul
snapshots.body: The pen name of Johann Paul Friedrich Richter, cited for having seen through Fichte's patriotic flattery of the Germans even though Goethe, Nietzsche guesses, judged the Germans differently.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose "lying but patriotic flatteries and exaggerations" about the German character Jean Paul is credited with seeing through.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
snapshots.body: Repeatedly paired with Napoleon as one of the "good Europeans": his prose is granted one exception to German stylistic clumsiness, his rewriting of Faust is tied to Napoleon's rise, his remark to Rath Schlosser on true esteem is quoted directly, and Napoleon's own astonishment on meeting him ("Voila un homme!") closes Chapter 7's parable of German skepticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
snapshots.body: Named again and again as the culmination of a European drama: the "absolute ruler" Europe's herd instinct craved, the man whose appearance changed Goethe's own Faust, the figure before whom Europe "danced round the Tree of Liberty" and then fell in adoration, and the one who told Madame de Stael to be silent in politics.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
snapshots.body: Named with Kant as one of the "philosophical workers" who systematize existing values rather than create new ones; also credited with having systematized the very riddles of the German soul that Wagner then set to music, and blamed by Schopenhauer's unintelligent rage for severing a whole generation from German culture.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heraclitus
snapshots.body: Named, with Plato and Empedocles, among the "royal and magnificent anchorites of the spirit" whose style of philosophy Nietzsche contrasts with the two "lions of Berlin" who pass for philosophers today.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Empedocles
snapshots.body: Named alongside Heraclitus and Plato as one of the ancient anchorites of the spirit against whom the modern philosophical pretenders of Berlin are measured and found wanting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugen Duhring
snapshots.body: One of the "two lions of Berlin" -- called "the anarchist" -- held up as an example of the hotch-potch "realist" or "positivist" philosophy that has replaced genuine philosophizing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eduard von Hartmann
snapshots.body: The other "lion of Berlin" -- called "the amalgamist" -- named alongside Eugen Duhring as an example of the diminished philosophy now passing for the real thing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
snapshots.body: Quoted for his motto "je ne meprise presque rien" (I despise almost nothing) -- Nietzsche's example of the "objective" or purely reflective spirit that affirms and denies nothing of its own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Michel de Montaigne
snapshots.body: Quoted for his signature question "What do I know?" -- one of the skeptic's consoling formulas, alongside Socrates' "I know that I know nothing."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jules Michelet
snapshots.body: The French historian credited with the phrase describing the German spirit as "cet esprit fataliste, ironique, mephistophelique" -- quoted as the outside verdict on a distinctly German kind of skepticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frederick the Great
snapshots.body: The King of Prussia whose "problematic, crazy father" doubted his manliness -- Nietzsche's parable for a new, harder, more dangerous German skepticism first entering Germany "in the person of the great Frederick"; a different Frederick from Chapter 6's Frederick II of Hohenstaufen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gustave Flaubert
snapshots.body: The "honest citizen of Rouen" whose lifelong preoccupation with bourgeois stupidity -- betise bourgeoise -- Nietzsche calls a mode of self-torment and refined cruelty.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame d'Epinay
snapshots.body: The addressee of a thoughtful letter from Galiani, cited as early documentary evidence of the overshadowing and "uglifying" of Europe that Nietzsche traces across the nineteenth century.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles de Saint-Evremond
snapshots.body: The seventeenth-century French critic named among those who could not fully appropriate Homer, reproaching him for his "esprit vaste" -- part of Nietzsche's argument that only the modern, hybrid "historical sense" can enjoy Homer without reservation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Voltaire
snapshots.body: Named repeatedly as the last echo of the classicizing century that still could not fully enjoy Homer; earlier apostrophized directly ("O Voltaire! O humanity! O idiocy!") over the naive idea that seeking truth serves the good.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The poet the modern "historical sense" can finally enjoy in full, where classical French taste (Saint-Evremond, Voltaire) could not -- Chapter 8's central test case for what a truly hybrid, omnivorous culture can appreciate that a purer one cannot.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Shakespeare
snapshots.body: Called a "marvelous Spanish-Moorish-Saxon synthesis of taste" that an ancient Athenian would have found laughable -- another of Chapter 8's proofs that only the modern, semi-barbarian European can enjoy such motley art without disturbance.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aeschylus
snapshots.body: Named as part of the "circle" of ancient Athenian taste against which Shakespeare's motley style is measured -- original-en's odd spelling "AEschylus" and modern-en's "Aeschylus" name the same Greek tragedian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jeremy Bentham
snapshots.body: The utilitarian philosopher whose footsteps English moralists are said to "stalk" in, just as he had earlier stalked in the footsteps of Helvetius -- part of Chapter 8's dismissal of English moral philosophy as tedious.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Claude Adrien Helvetius
snapshots.body: The Enlightenment philosopher Bentham is said to have followed -- quoted secondhand via Galiani's witticism calling him "ce senateur Pococurante" (that senator who cares for nothing), borrowing the name of Voltaire's blase character in Candide rather than naming a real Pococurante.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame de Lambert
snapshots.body: The eighteenth-century salon hostess whose remark to her son -- "never permit yourself follies except ones that will give you great pleasure" -- Nietzsche calls the wisest and most motherly thing ever said to a son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dante Alighieri
snapshots.body: Named with Goethe as sharing a belief about woman that Nietzsche expects every noble woman to reject -- quoted in the original Italian, "Ella guardava suso, ed io in lei."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame de Stael
