snapshots.body: The writer Napoleon is said to have told, in Latin, to keep quiet in politics ("mulier taceat in politicis"); also one of three women (with Madame Roland and George Sand) a woman should not cite as proof of her sex's capacities.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Madame Roland
snapshots.body: The French revolutionary-era writer named, with Madame de Stael and George Sand, as one of "three comical women" no one should cite as an argument for feminine emancipation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: David Hume
snapshots.body: The skeptic Kant is said to have risen up against; named, with Hobbes and Locke, among the three Englishmen whose mechanical philosophy Nietzsche blames for a century of philosophical abasement.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thomas Hobbes
snapshots.body: Named with Hume and Locke as one of the three Englishmen responsible for depreciating the very idea of "philosopher"; quoted again in Chapter 10 for calling laughter a "bad infirmity of human nature."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Locke
snapshots.body: Named at 2:19 for a "superficiality" about the origin of ideas Nietzsche says his own account corrects, and again at 9:12 with Hobbes and Hume as one of the English trio blamed for abasing philosophy -- quoted secondhand there via Schelling's dismissive French, "Je meprise Locke."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thomas Carlyle
snapshots.body: Called "the absurd muddle-head" and "half-actor and rhetorician" whose passionate grimaces conceal exactly what England lacks: real depth of intellect, i.e. philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Francis Bacon
snapshots.body: Named as representing, by himself, an "attack on the philosophical spirit generally" -- the opening figure in Chapter 9's roll call of English thinkers Nietzsche holds responsible for depreciating philosophy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demosthenes
snapshots.body: Named with Cicero as an orator whose long, breath-spanning periods -- possible only because ancient audiences still read aloud -- modern readers, short of breath in every sense, no longer have any right to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.body: Named with Demosthenes as a master of the classical, breath-defined period, part of Chapter 9's argument that German prose has lost its ear because Germans no longer read aloud.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charles Darwin
snapshots.body: Named, with John Stuart Mill and Herbert Spencer, as one of the "respectable but mediocre Englishmen" whose ascendancy in European taste Nietzsche treats as symptomatic rather than triumphant, even while granting that English narrowness suited his specific discoveries.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Stuart Mill
snapshots.body: Named with Darwin and Herbert Spencer as one of the mediocre Englishmen whose truths appeal specifically to mediocre minds.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Herbert Spencer
snapshots.body: Named with Darwin and Mill as the third of Chapter 9's mediocre but ascendant Englishmen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich von Sybel
snapshots.body: The German historian named, pluralized ("the Sybels"), as one type-example of the "Prussian folly" -- historians with, Nietzsche says, "closely bandaged heads."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich von Treitschke
snapshots.body: The nationalist historian named, pluralized ("the Treitschkes"), alongside Sybel as the other type-example of Prussian historical folly.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich Heine
snapshots.body: Named as having been "reincarnated" in the refined, fastidious lyrists of Paris -- one of the German exports France has quietly absorbed -- and later grouped among the "good Europeans" whose real allegiance outran their fatherlands.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippolyte Taine
snapshots.body: The French historian in whose work Hegel's influence is said now to exercise an almost tyrannical dominance over French thought -- called "the first of living historians."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Victor Hugo
snapshots.body: The writer whose funeral is cited as the occasion for a "veritable orgy of bad taste" and national self-admiration, evidence for Nietzsche of France's current besottedness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stendhal
snapshots.body: The pen name of Henri Beyle, called "the last great psychologist of France": named as Stendhal for his aphorism that a good philosopher must be dry, clear, without illusion (Chapter 3), and as Henri Beyle for his Napoleonic tempo in surveying the European soul two generations ahead of his readers (Chapter 9).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Richard Wagner
snapshots.body: The composer whose overture to the Meistersinger opens Chapter 9's long study of German music; his Kundry (Chapter 3) staged the religious neurosis as Schopenhauerian confession, his riddles of the German soul are said to be the ones Hegel had already systematized, and the chapter's climax names him -- alongside Napoleon and Goethe -- among the handful of true "good Europeans," his Siegfried and Parsifal both weighed at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
snapshots.body: Contrasted at length with Mozart as the "intermediate event" between an old mellow soul and a future over-young one -- his music carries, Nietzsche says, the same twilight of loss and hope in which Europe dreamed with Rousseau and danced toward Napoleon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
snapshots.body: Called the last echo of a great, centuries-old European taste -- his rococo delicacy, tenderness, and belief in the South are said still to speak to something left in "us," unlike Beethoven's more fragile appeal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
snapshots.body: Named as the starting point of the historical arc Beethoven's music is said to carry -- Europe "dreamed with Rousseau" before dancing around the Tree of Liberty and falling into adoration of Napoleon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Friedrich Schiller
snapshots.body: Named among the poets (with Rousseau, Shelley and Byron) whose language now sounds strange to modern ears despite once voicing the same European fate Beethoven's music sang; a footnote in original-en also traces one phrase to his play William Tell.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
snapshots.body: Named with Rousseau, Schiller and Byron as one of the Romantic poets whose collective voice, once able to speak Europe's fate, now sounds difficult to fully grasp.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lord Byron
snapshots.body: Named among the Romantic poets whose voice has faded from modern ears; his Manfred is also the basis for the Schumann composition Nietzsche calls a "mistake and a misunderstanding," and he appears again in Chapter 10 among the great poets whose "work" invented the men later reverenced as their authors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Carl Maria von Weber
snapshots.body: The composer of Der Freischutz and Oberon, named as belonging to a Romanticism already extinct, though not yet forgotten, in German music.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heinrich Marschner
snapshots.body: The composer of Hans Heiling and Der Vampyr, grouped with Weber as another representative of the fading Romantic school of German opera.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Felix Mendelssohn
snapshots.body: Called "that halcyon master," whose lighter, purer, happier soul won quick admiration and was just as quickly forgotten -- the "beautiful episode" of German music.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robert Schumann
snapshots.body: The composer treated at length as the point where German music became merely national rather than European: his Manfred is called a mistake, his taste "fundamentally petty," and his "surmounting" a relief precisely because it ends a danger Beethoven and Mozart never posed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Siegfried
snapshots.body: The hero of Wagner's Ring, called Wagner's most remarkable, permanently inimitable creation -- "too free, too hard, too cheerful, too healthy" for the taste of older, more mellow civilizations, and, Nietzsche says, almost a sin against Romanticism.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugene Delacroix
snapshots.body: Named as the artist nearest related to Wagner among the great European Romantics -- grouped with Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heine and Schopenhauer as one who outgrew any single fatherland.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Honore de Balzac
snapshots.body: Cited near the start of Chapter 7 for the phrase "montrer ses plaies" (to show one's wounds); named again in Chapter 9 as an example of the tireless, self-destroying worker unable to achieve a noble tempo or lento in life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Georges Bizet
snapshots.body: The composer credited with having made music "for" the "good Europeans" who love both North and South at once -- his work is called the discovery of "a piece of the South in music."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
snapshots.body: Discussed at greater length than almost anyone else in the book: his account of the will is picked apart in Chapter 1, his pessimism is the background of Chapter 3's religious crisis (with Wagner's Kundry its "genuine Schopenhauerian consequence"), Chapter 6 quotes his Grundprobleme der Ethik at length and notes, drily, that this repudiator of God still played the flute every day after dinner, and Chapter 9 counts him among the true "good Europeans."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Rath Schlosser
snapshots.body: Johann Georg Schlosser, Goethe's brother-in-law and the addressee of the letter Nietzsche quotes as Chapter 10's epigraph: "One can only truly esteem him who does not look out for himself."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Raphael
snapshots.body: Invoked in the phrase "Raphael without hands" -- Nietzsche's figure for genius that lacks the sheer number of hands needed to seize the right moment.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Horace
snapshots.body: Quoted in Latin ("naturam expellere... usque recurret") on the impossibility of driving out nature with a pitchfork -- cited as the source any truthfulness-preaching educator would eventually have to reach for.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dr. Marianus
snapshots.body: The character from Goethe's Faust, Part II, whose line -- "Here is the prospect free, the mind exalted" -- is quoted (with attribution given only in a footnote) to introduce the reverse kind of man who is also on a height but looks downward.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysus
snapshots.body: The god who names himself only near the close of Chapter 10 as "the tempter-god and born rat-catcher of consciences" -- Nietzsche's own last disciple and initiate, distinct from the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse named in Chapter 1.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariadne
snapshots.body: Named as present at Dionysus's side when the god confesses, "under certain circumstances I love mankind" -- the mythic consort Nietzsche would return to repeatedly in his later notebooks.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Sphinx
snapshots.body: The riddling monster of the Oedipus myth, twice personified as a figure of dangerous, ambiguous knowledge -- "which of us is the Oedipus here? Which the Sphinx?" in the Preface's opening pages, and "the Sphinx, too, is a Circe" in Chapter 7.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oedipus
snapshots.body: Named twice as the figure of fearless, unblinking insight: paired with the Sphinx in the Preface's opening question about who is asking whom, and again in Chapter 8's image of "fearless Oedipus-eyes" turned on nature itself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zarathustra
snapshots.body: Nietzsche's own prophet-figure from Thus Spoke Zarathustra, named in the closing poem's final stanza as the long-awaited "Guest of Guests" whose arrival ends the poem's long, lonely waiting.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: Named for the constellation, not the labors: Nietzsche says he is pleased to hear the sun is moving rapidly toward it, and hopes "good Europeans" will do likewise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wotan
snapshots.body: The Norse/Germanic god quoted via an old Scandinavian saga -- "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast" -- Nietzsche's chosen epigraph for the proud, self-mastering Viking soul at the center of master-morality.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pallas Athene
snapshots.body: The Greek goddess invoked as the figure Spinoza's mathematical "mail and mask" was meant to terrify any assailant away from approaching, as though she were an "invincible maiden."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.
